The horn version of [Patterns by Ear](patterns-by-ear.qmd). The first few patterns of a set are taught with lever diagrams.
Then the page plays the rest, one at a time, and you play each back on your horn. New to the fingerings? See the
[horn page](../lessons/horn.qmd#explore).

```{=html}
<div class="ep-panel">
  <div class="ep-dots" id="eh-dots2"></div>

  <div class="ep-solf" id="eh-ear-solf"></div>

  <p class="ep-muted">The key is played first (I – V7 – I). Then each pattern: listen, then play it back. A wrong note stops the

</div>
```

## How it works {#how}

- **Written notes.** Everything on this page is in *written* pitch, the notes on your part. The page plays them at the
  pitch the horn really sounds (a perfect fifth lower than written), and the microphone turns what it hears back into written notes.
- **Range.** Each set is moved to the written key you pick and placed between written C4 and G5 when it fits. That range is a rule of thumb for
  a first-year player, not from the book (unverified).
- **Levers.** The usual fingering from the [horn chart](../lessons/horn.qmd#explore). On a double horn the page shows the F side below written
  G♯4/A♭4 and the B♭ side (thumb down) from there up, the switch point the book recommends. Your teacher may prefer something else.
- **What counts.** The notes in order; rhythm isn't checked. Each new note must hold steady for about a tenth of a second. To play the
  same note twice, stop the sound briefly between them (tongue it). With *Any octave counts* on, the whole pattern may be an octave away.
  Stopping for more than four seconds starts the try again.
- **The microphone** ignores everything while the page is playing. Headphones still help. Low horn notes are hard for pitch detection, so
  a wrong octave is common: leave *Any octave counts* on.
- **No horn handy?** A MIDI keyboard or wind controller, or the computer keys, count as written notes.

**For students**

"French horn." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_horn). Unverified: that a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below written pitch, and the sizes the levers lower the pitch (1 whole step, 2 half step, 3 step and a half). Not yet re-read.

**For teachers**

"Horn." Teacher resource book, Neil A. Kjos Music Company (item W74; title and authors unverified), pp. 176-89. Scan pages checked: history, instrument family p. 176; selecting players and parts diagram p. 183; assembly, posture, hand position p. 184; notes on posture and embouchure p. 185; daily care p. 186; oiling and greasing p. 187; stringing a rotary valve p. 188; Horn Fingering Chart (written pitch, treble clef, F3-C6: F-horn fingering on top, B-flat horn in brackets, 'use either on a double horn', switch at G-sharp4/A-flat4) p. 189. The Tone Production Problems and Remedies table is read from the scan's printed p. 169 (trumpet chapter). No tuning section for horn in the pages seen. Retold in the page's own words; the lever picture is traced from a three-lever template (horn.ai), the thumb lever is the page's own. Printed page numbers of the chart page and of the pages with clipped headers are unverified.
